doc.title: Denny Zeitlin interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: Reluctance to record and playing at Illinois and Hopkins
summary: Musicians' horror stories about labels made him disinterested in recording; he played with many musicians at Illinois and sat in with Gary Bartz in Baltimore.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: talk to me about what was going on at home and what was bothering them and I would just listen. And I had a model early on, I had an uncle who was a psychoanalyst in Chicago. And he started talking with me about his work very early. And my mother had incredible psychological radar. She could just read people. Extraordinary sensitivity to nuances of emotional states, how people were put together. So those two influences were very strong in me. So early on I had an idea I wanted to be a doctor. My father was a doctor. I wanted to be a psychiatrist. I knew I wanted to play music. I didn’t know exactly what shape my musical involvement would take or how public it might ever become, but I knew I was going to be involved in music all my life. But I didn’t really set out, like in high school, that I wanted definitely to have any sort of big public career as a musician. I started playing professionally in high school, in jazz bands, and started sitting in. But I mean I didn’t have big aspirations to start recording for instance. And possibly that was influenced by a number of musicians who were then on the scene and who were recording, who were telling me horror stories about record labels. About how their music was subverted. How they weren’t allowed to play what they really wanted. How corrupt the marketplace was. So that there was a kind of atmosphere created that the really pure artistic thing to do was not to even bother with recording.
